keep: The idea is named in one line up front with the Bitesize formula [1], and the derivation is lesson 4's moves with letters, line by line, footnoted to MathWorld's a(x + b/2a)² + (c − b²/4a) [2].
The course brief's anchor is used: x² + 6x + 2 = 0 through the formula, 28, √28 = 2√7 (the surd step from Powers and roots), back to −3 ± √7, about −0.35 and −5.65, as lesson 4 found.
The picture is the brief's centre and spread: the dashed axis at −b ÷ 2a, two equal arrows of √(b² − 4ac) ÷ 2a, a b² − 4ac readout, and 'no real roots' in ink once it goes negative.

Thirteen screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), ending on three mixed puzzles (11-13); every lesson-5 mistake in the brief has a screen with its own wrong pick: the ± dropped (2, 4), the slips in b² − 4ac (6), roots found from a negative discriminant (8), the nature of the roots (10, 13), surds (5), choosing the method (11).

fix: Causal step skipped (why lifting shrinks the arrows): the explanation says the discriminant 36 − 4c falls but not why that is the same thing as lesson 4. Add: x² + 6x + c = 0 becomes (x + 3)² = 9 − c, and 36 − 4c is 4 × (9 − c), so lifting the curve asks the square to make a smaller number, then 0 at c = 9, then a negative it cannot make. Also say why the curve just touches: its lowest point is c − 9, which is 0 at c = 9.
False absolute in practice: '−4ac turns positive when a or c is negative' is wrong when both are negative (a = −1, c = −2 gives −4ac = −8). Say 'when just one of a and c is negative'.

False absolutes: 'you never have to do it again' and 'the formula, which always works' overreach. Say you need not do it each time, and that the formula works on every quadratic, telling you when there are no real roots.
Misconception not shown failing in the explanation: 'drop it and you lose a root' is a claim. Show it: x² + 6x + 5 = 0 with only + gives −1, and −5 works too: 25 − 30 + 5 = 0.

Rule not stated in words: give the formula once as words (minus b, plus or minus the square root of b squared take away 4ac, all over 2a) so 'all over' carries the whole-top point the slip screen tests.
'b² ÷ 4a − c over one bottom number is (b² − 4ac) ÷ 4a' skips the step: say c is 4ac ÷ 4a.

The brief asks every lesson for a 'spot the slip' screen; screen 4 only compares three formulas. Make it a worked wrong answer of x² + 6x + 5 = 0 with only the square root over 2a, and ask which line slipped.

The last screen should point to Complex numbers, as the brief says (lesson 5 ends with a clean 'no real roots' and a pointer). Name it in screen 13 and in one sentence of explain, on Brilliant's 'non-real complex roots only' [3], without teaching it.
Screens 11-13 are not described for the builder; name each equation and what the picks are.
Analogy breaks: 'between them its graph is on the other side of the axis' is vague; say it dips below the axis between the roots when a is positive.
